A "fragment" annotation on d1o5dt2 doesn't change its classification. It changes how you use the domain as data.

What the SCOPe 2.08 API shows (current release, found via /api/v1/releases):
- d1uc6a1 (sunid 107766, "1uc6 A:6-109") is in b.1.2.1, Fibronectin type III family (sunid 49266). Its protein is ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor alpha (sunid 110060), species human.
- d1o5dt2 (sunid 103884, "1o5d T:107-205") is also in b.1.2.1. Its protein is the extracellular region of human tissue factor (sunid 49267), species human.
- Both sit under the same family node, 49266, in fold b.1 (immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich), superfamily b.1.2 (fibronectin type III), class b (all-beta).
- The API node records I retrieved did not show an explicit "fragment" flag. I take the fragment status from your prompt. I could only confirm that d1o5dt2 is a defined sub-range (107-205) of chain T, not a whole chain.

What family membership means here. Both domains belong to the family because SCOPe judged them to have a close evolutionary relationship, based on structure and sequence or functional evidence. The two are different proteins, a cytokine receptor and tissue factor, so same-family membership does not mean they share function, ligand binding, or biology. It does not make either a template for the other's interface or epitopes. Being in the same family is also not the same as being the same protein or species-level instance.

Alignment:
- Do not treat the fragment as a full-length FnIII domain. A truncated or partial domain may lack edge strands or termini. Alignments to it can show gaps or terminal mismatches that come from missing structure, not evolutionary divergence.
- Align on the structurally defined core (beta-sandwich strands) and use structure-aware or profile alignment.
- Check the observed residue ranges and any missing density against the other domain. Do not infer insertions, deletions or loop length differences from the fragment's termini.
- Compare d1o5dt2 (99 residues, 107-205) with d1uc6a1 (104 residues, 6-109) over the common core only, and report coverage.

Representative selection:
- Prefer complete, well-resolved, non-fragment domains as family representatives or templates, for example for modeling or benchmarking. This holds unless the fragment is the only available instance of a protein or species.
- Choose representatives per protein or species node, not per family. The two domains are from different proteins, so each can represent its own protein, and neither should stand in for the whole family.
- Do not select a fragment merely because it shares the family label. Also avoid choosing it because it has a close sequence neighbor or comes from a larger complex. Check resolution, completeness, construct boundaries and redundancy (for example, the many d2b7dt2-like tissue factor entries) before selecting.
- Treat any fragment-based representative as provisional, and say the representative may be incomplete.

Family diversity:
- Counting domains, entries or fragments inflates apparent diversity. Fragments and redundant structures of the same protein (here many tissue factor chains) add entries without adding evolutionary diversity.
- Measure diversity at the protein and species levels, and cluster by sequence identity. Count a fragment only if it adds a distinct protein or sequence.
- Partial domains can also under-represent a family, because missing regions hide real loop and strand variation.
- Two members in b.1.2.1 do not show the family is small or homogeneous. FnIII is a very large, diverse family, and evolutionary distance within it can be large. Do not extrapolate from two members.

Limits: the fragment annotation is a data-quality caveat, not evidence of a different fold or family. Confirm construct boundaries and completeness against the PDB entry (1o5d chain T, 1uc6 chain A) or the SCOPe domain pages before relying on either domain.

- d1uc6a1 (sunid 107766, "1uc6 A:6-109") is in b.1.2.1, Fibronectin type III family (sunid 49266). Its protein is ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor alpha (sunid 110060), species human.
- d1o5dt2 (sunid 103884, "1o5d T:107-205") is also in b.1.2.1. Its protein is the extracellular region of human tissue factor (sunid 49267), species human.
- Both sit under the same family node, 49266, in fold b.1 (immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich), superfamily b.1.2 (fibronectin type III), class b (all-beta).
- The API node records I retrieved did not show an explicit "fragment" flag. I take the fragment status from your prompt. I could only confirm that d1o5dt2 is a defined sub-range (107-205) of chain T, not a whole chain.

What family membership means here. Both domains belong to the family because SCOPe judged them to have a close evolutionary relationship, based on structure and sequence or functional evidence. The two are different proteins, a cytokine receptor and tissue factor, so same-family membership does not mean they share function, ligand binding, or biology. It does not make either a template for the other's interface or epitopes. Being in the same family is also not the same as being the same protein or species-level instance.

Alignment:
- Do not treat the fragment as a full-length FnIII domain. A truncated or partial domain may lack edge strands or termini. Alignments to it can show gaps or terminal mismatches that come from missing structure, not evolutionary divergence.
- Align on the structurally defined core (beta-sandwich strands) and use structure-aware or profile alignment.
- Check the observed residue ranges and any missing density against the other domain. Do not infer insertions, deletions or loop length differences from the fragment's termini.
- Compare d1o5dt2 (99 residues, 107-205) with d1uc6a1 (104 residues, 6-109) over the common core only, and report coverage.

Representative selection:
- Prefer complete, well-resolved, non-fragment domains as family representatives or templates, for example for modeling or benchmarking. This holds unless the fragment is the only available instance of a protein or species.
- Choose representatives per protein or species node, not per family. The two domains are from different proteins, so each can represent its own protein, and neither should stand in for the whole family.
- Do not select a fragment merely because it shares the family label. Also avoid choosing it because it has a close sequence neighbor or comes from a larger complex. Check resolution, completeness, construct boundaries and redundancy (for example, the many d2b7dt2-like tissue factor entries) before selecting.
- Treat any fragment-based representative as provisional, and say the representative may be incomplete.

Family diversity:
- Counting domains, entries or fragments inflates apparent diversity. Fragments and redundant structures of the same protein (here many tissue factor chains) add entries without adding evolutionary diversity.
- Measure diversity at the protein and species levels, and cluster by sequence identity. Count a fragment only if it adds a distinct protein or sequence.
- Partial domains can also under-represent a family, because missing regions hide real loop and strand variation.
- Two members in b.1.2.1 do not show the family is small or homogeneous. FnIII is a very large, diverse family, and evolutionary distance within it can be large. Do not extrapolate from two members.

Limits: the fragment annotation is a data-quality caveat, not evidence of a different fold or family. Confirm construct boundaries and completeness against the PDB entry (1o5d chain T, 1uc6 chain A) or the SCOPe domain pages before relying on either domain.
